newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FEATURE-S.African elite unit ready to return to hot spots.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-S.African elite unit ready to return to hot spots.

text.p: South Africa's special forces, which wreaked havoc in neighbouring countries during the apartheid war, are ready to return to the continent's hot spots -- but this time on the side of the angels.
As ethnic fighting spread in Zaire in recent days, the commander of South Africa's 5 Special Forces Regiment, Colonel Julius Engelbrecht, told reporters:
"I cannot foresee that South Africa will stay out of peace operations. There will be a need for reconnaissance, and we will do it...It is part of the planning of the defence force."

The government has taken no decision on whether it would join in an African peacekeeping force, but leading defence spokesman Tony Yengeni of President Nelson Mandela's African National Congress (ANC) said on Monday there was strong support for the idea.

"We have an obligation to participate in efforts to maintain stability in the continent but it has to be part of a clear policy and it would have to be endorsed by the United Nations, the Organisation of African Unity and the Southern African Development Community," Yengeni said.

Engelbrecht spoke during a rare media visit recently to the regiment's base at Phalaborwa near the border with Mozambique, organised to show that the secretive unit had nothing to hide from the range of investigators now probing apartheid crimes.
"We are supporting the government of the day," Engelbrecht said. "We never got involved in unauthorised operations."

He said his unit played a key role in a turning point in recent South African history when about 5,000 armed right-wing whites tried to take over part of the nominally independent Bophuthatswana homeland in the weeks before the April 1994 democratic elections.

"We escorted them out of there, and we told them not to come back or they would be in a firefight," Engelbrecht said. The humiliation of the right-wingers marked the end of the white right as a potential threat to the country's peaceful transition.

Engelbrecht declined to give the size of the unit but it is composed mainly of black "operators" who undergo a rigorous 49-week selection course that includes training in demolition, survival skills and parachute jumping. An average of 90 percent of volunteers for the course fail it.

The unit, permanently on six-hour standby, developed from one set up in 1976 in which black troops were trained to infiltrate liberation groups like the ANC -- now the ruling party -- and the South West African People's Organisation (SWAPO) which was fighting Pretoria's control of what is now Namibia.
Engelbrecht said unit members had an average of 15 years combat experience each, much of it in Angola during the war against SWAPO and their Cuban allies.

He said the regiment had lost about 60 or 70 operators and support staff to Executive Outcomes, the private Pretoria-based mercenary company which has provided military training and support for the governments of Angola and Sierra Leone.

"We were sorry to lose them, but we can't match the Executive Outcomes pay...We are very short of men," Engelbrecht said, adding that the high standards set for entry into the unit meant few soldiers could qualify.
"We can compare with the best in the world...Be sure we can do our job."
He said that members of the regiment spoke 24 African languages between them but not French, which he acknowledged was a weakness.
Facilities at the Phalaborwa base include a windowless room painted with anti-apartheid graffiti like "Viva SWAPO" and "Kill the Boers".

"We used this in the old days for 'dark phase' training," an officer said. "It is meant to simulate capture by the ANC or SWAPO, so operators would be prepared for attempts to turn them if they fell into enemy hands."
"Dark Phase" training included campfire sessions where operators would sing the ANC's anti-apartheid liberation songs.
